blocks.text: If you write grants on a Mac, Gmail is probably where a large part of your day goes. You send drafts to program officers, chase budget files from collaborators, and answer the same questions every week. Gmail can handle much of that without help. This guide covers the built-in features first. Then it shows where Lazur fits.
Why grant writers spend so much time in email

Email often works as the filing cabinet for grant work. A March 2026 survey by Instrumentl asked 1,031 grant professionals about their week. The survey was not a random sample. Instrumentl sells software to grant teams, so read it as a signal, not a verdict. Even so, the numbers match what many writers see at their desks.

The typical respondent reported 29.5 hours a week on manual, repetitive tasks. Sixty-five percent said they spend as much time managing processes as they do on strategic work. And 68% said they use email folders as the system of record for grant documents. Those three figures point to one fix. Make Gmail handle the repeated work, so your attention goes to the proposal.

The lost time is not only in sending. You lose it searching for the right PDF, rewriting the same reminder, and checking whether a deadline moved. The sections below take those jobs one at a time, starting with the features that save the most effort.
Turn on Gmail templates before you need them

Templates are the fastest win for most grant writers. Google's help page says you can only turn on and use templates from Gmail on your computer. You cannot switch them on from the Gmail app on your phone, so do it at your desk.

items: Open Gmail in Safari or Chrome on your Mac, then click the gear icon at the top right.
Scroll to the bottom of the page and click Save Changes.

blocks.text: Google's steps describe a computer, not a specific Mac menu, so the labels can shift after a browser update. Look for the Advanced tab and the Templates setting. The path stays the same even when the layout changes a little.
Build four templates for the emails you repeat

Start with four templates. Most grant writers send the same few kinds of email. Good first picks are an inquiry follow-up, a cover note for a letter of intent, a reporting reminder, and a thank-you after a decision.

To save one, write the email in a compose window. Click More options, the three dots at the bottom of the window. Choose Templates, then Save draft as template, then Save as new template. Pick a name you will still recognize in six months.
Avoid the two template mistakes that cost the most

The first mistake is overwriting. Google's help page says updating a template uses Overwrite Template. That replaces the old text. If you want to keep the original, save the changed version as a new template with a new name first.
The second mistake is deleting too fast. Google says you cannot recover a template after you delete it. Before you remove one, copy its text into a note. A folder of old drafts works well for this.

Keep funder names out of the body text. Use brackets such as [Funder name] and [due date]. Then search for the brackets before you send. A template that still names the last funder is a common and embarrassing error.
Use a filter when a template must answer automatically

Google's help page says that to send a template as an automatic reply, you must create a filter. This matters for a shared grants inbox, where the same question arrives from several people. A filter can catch mail from a set sender and answer it with the right template.

Test the filter with a message from a second account you control. Read the reply that comes back before you let the filter run for a week. Filters only act on mail that matches them, so a narrow rule is safer than a broad one.
The filter steps are on our page: [How to create a filter in Gmail on Mac](/how-to/create-a-filter-in-gmail).
Send attachments without hitting the size limit

A personal Gmail account has a total attachment cap of 25 MB. If the attachments go over that cap, Gmail removes them and adds a Google Drive link to the email. Work or school accounts follow the limit their admin sets.

blocks.title: Work accounts differ
blocks.text: Work or school Gmail accounts follow the attachment limit their admin sets. Ask IT before a large send, and do not assume the 25 MB personal limit applies to you.

Think about the full package before you attach anything. A narrative, a budget workbook and several letters of support can exceed the cap together, even when each file looks small. Count the total, not each file.

Put the folder in Google Drive, then share it with the program officer. Name the final version clearly, such as Final budget, not budget 3 final. Link to it in the body. Check the sharing setting before you send. A link that only you can open helps nobody.

The attachment steps for the browser are on our page: [How to attach a file in Gmail on Mac](/how-to/attach-a-file-in-gmail). If your university or nonprofit account has a different limit, ask your IT team. A file that bounces on deadline day costs more than a short question now.
Schedule email in Gmail on Mac for deadlines and time zones

Scheduled sends help when a funder works in another time zone, or when you finish a draft late at night. Google's scheduling help page says you can have up to 100 scheduled emails. It also says a scheduled email may send a few minutes after the time you chose.
That few-minute delay matters. Never schedule a submission for the exact minute of the deadline. Schedule it well before the deadline, and leave yourself time to check the sent copy.

Google's scheduling page covers the phone steps. The browser steps are on our page: [How to schedule an email to send later in Gmail](/how-to/schedule-an-email-to-send-later-in-gmail). Use those steps, then check the scheduled folder before you walk away.
A worked example: one week of funder email

Take a typical week. On Monday, a program officer asks for a deadline extension. You want a short, polite reply that you can send after you check the calendar. Open the template with the extension wording, fill in the brackets, and schedule the send for Tuesday morning.

On Tuesday, a collaborator sends the budget as three files, and Gmail says the total is too large. You move the files into a Drive folder, set view access, and paste the link into a reply. You label the thread with the grant name, so it does not get lost in the inbox.

On Thursday, you search for every PDF from the funder in the last month. A search for the funder's address with the filename operator returns the list fast. You snooze the reporting reminder until the Friday before it is due.

Nothing in that week needed a new tool. It needed templates, one label, a Drive folder, a search and a snooze. Lazur helps with the parts you cannot see at a glance, such as which setting you need next.
Label and filter funder email so it stops piling up

Labels are how Gmail groups mail. A label for each active grant works better than one catch-all folder. Put the funder's name in the label, then add a proposal number if you have one. A short list of labels is easier to scan than a long one.

Filters do the sorting for you. You might set one that labels mail from a funder's domain and skips the inbox. Only do this for mail you read in one place, or you will miss a message. The label steps are on our page: [How to create a label in Gmail on Mac](/how-to/create-a-label-in-gmail).
A new filter sorts new mail by default. Old messages stay where they are unless you tick the option to apply the filter to matching conversations. Tick it when you want the old mail sorted too.
Search Gmail for the attachment you need
You search for the same few things over and over. Gmail's search bar accepts operators that narrow the results fast. Type them into the search bar at the top of the window.

items: has:attachment shows messages with a file attached.
filename:pdf shows messages with a PDF attached.
from:name@example.org shows mail from one sender.
Combine them, such as has:attachment from:name@example.org budget, to narrow the search.

blocks.text: Search is faster than scrolling through a long thread. For more examples, see [How to search emails with attachments in Gmail on Mac](/how-to/search-emails-with-attachments-in-gmail).
Where Lazur fits in your Gmail window

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac that lives in the notch. Hold ⌥ ⌘, which is Option and Command together, to ask about anything on screen. Lazur answers out loud. It looks at your screen only while you hold the shortcut, so it can see the Gmail window in your browser.

Lazur does not click buttons, edit files, or operate other apps for you. You stay in control of every send. Lazur points, explains, guides, drafts and types text. It is not a plugin or add-in for Gmail, and Lazur has no partnerships with any app maker.
Ask Lazur where a Gmail control is

Gmail changes its layout from time to time. Many people spend minutes hunting for one option. Ask Lazur instead. Ask where the send options are, and Lazur draws a circle and a label around the control on your screen.

When you want steps, ask Lazur to walk you through it. Lazur guides you one click at a time and waits for each click. That helps with settings such as turning on templates, where one wrong tab wastes ten minutes.
Draft and dictate replies, then read every line

Lazur drafts and types text. Ask for a short reply, and it types the draft at your cursor. The draft is a starting point. A program officer will notice a wrong deadline, a missing name, or a tone that does not fit the relationship.
Give Lazur real facts in the request. Name the funder, the date, the request and the tone you want. It writes from what you say and from what is on screen, so vague prompts get vague replies.

Hold fn to dictate clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app. Dictation suits long narrative replies you would rather speak than type. Dictation is included with Lazur, so you can use it on the same plan as the rest of the features.
Fix names with a personal dictionary and snippets

Funder names, program acronyms and co-applicant names often come out wrong when you dictate them. Add them to Lazur's personal dictionary once. After that, the spelling is right every time you dictate them.
Snippets help with the parts you repeat. Save a standard closing paragraph, a short line about your organization, or a signature block. Then dictate the new content around it.
Dictation is only as good as your last read. Scan the text before you send, especially numbers, dates and dollar amounts. A wrong figure in a budget email is hard to walk back.
Common Gmail mistakes grant writers make

items: Replying all to a whole review panel when only the program officer needed the answer.
Sending a reused template that still names the last funder.
Scheduling a submission for the exact minute of the deadline.
Attaching a large file when a Drive link would work better.
Sharing a Drive link with a setting that blocks the reader.
Assuming a phone can build your templates. It cannot.
Deleting an old template to tidy up, then needing it the next week.

blocks.text: Undo Send and recall: what you can count on

Gmail offers Undo Send, but its window is short. Do not plan on it to fix a wrong attachment or a wrong recipient. Our recall page explains what works: [How to recall an email in Gmail on Mac](/how-to/recall-a-sent-email-in-gmail).

A better habit is a short check before you send. Confirm the recipient, the attachment name and the deadline. In Gmail on a Mac browser, ⌘ Return sends the draft from the keyboard once you are satisfied. A checklist saved in a template keeps the steps the same every time.
Use reminders and snoozes for funder deadlines

Instrumentl's survey found 82% of respondents use email and calendar reminders. That fits what many writers already do. The trick is to make the reminder land on the day you need to act, not the day you first read the email.

Snooze a message until the day it needs action. The steps for Safari and Chrome are on our page: [How to snooze an email in Gmail on Mac](/how-to/snooze-an-email-in-gmail). For a hard due date, add a calendar event, or ask Lazur to add an Apple Reminders item for the day before.

Email time adds up across a week. Mailbird's survey of more than 250 professionals found about a third spend 3 to 5 hours a week managing email. Mailbird sells an email app, and its dates in the write-up do not agree, so treat it as a rough guide.
How long grant writing takes, and where email fits

Email time sits inside a larger block of hours. Instrumentl's article on finding grants includes a table on writing time. In that table, 41.30% of respondents said a grant application takes 10 to 20 hours. The table had about 46 answers, so use it as a rough signal, not a fact about every grant.

The same article advises turning off email notifications during focused work. For a grant writer, that advice is the easiest one to act on. Turn off mail alerts while you draft, then check the inbox at set times.
Your first week with Gmail for grant writing

Do the setup in this order. Turn on templates. Save four templates. Create one label for each open grant. Add one filter for the funder that sends the most mail. Ask Lazur to explain anything on screen that you do not understand.
Then stop adding. Use the setup for two weeks before you add more. Most grant writers find that the first week shows which steps they repeat, and those are the only ones worth automating.
When you want a voice assistant on the Mac that helps inside Gmail, start with the free trial. It needs no credit card. Plans and prices are on our [pricing page](/pricing).

faq.question: Is there a separate Gmail app for Mac?
faq.answer: Google's help pages describe Gmail on a computer, and most grant writers use it in Safari or Chrome. Check Google's help site before you install any newer app. Lazur works with the Gmail window in your browser.

faq.question: Can I make Gmail templates on my iPhone?
faq.answer: No. Google's help page says you can only turn on and use templates from Gmail on a computer. Set them up at your Mac, then use Gmail as you normally do.

faq.question: How big can an attachment be in Gmail?
faq.answer: A personal Gmail account has a total attachment cap of 25 MB. Work or school accounts follow the limit their admin sets. When attachments go over the cap, Gmail adds a Google Drive link instead.

faq.question: How many emails can I schedule in Gmail?
faq.answer: Google's scheduling help page says you can have up to 100 scheduled emails. A scheduled email may send a few minutes after the time you chose, so schedule it well before any deadline.

faq.question: Can Lazur send my emails for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not click buttons or operate other apps for you. It points, explains, guides, drafts and types text. You read the draft and send it yourself.

faq.question: Does Lazur send my screen or audio to AI providers?
faq.answer: Lazur listens and looks at your screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer you, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models.

faq.question: Is Lazur an add-in for Gmail?
faq.answer: No. Lazur is not a plugin or add-in for any app, and it has no partnerships with any app maker. It works alongside whatever is open on your Mac.

faq.question: Why did my template overwrite my old text?
faq.answer: Updating a template uses Overwrite Template, which replaces the saved text. Save a changed version under a new name first, and keep a copy of any template you may need again.
